core: working definition: a mode of subsistence is the way people interact with their environments in order to make a living (attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology 7.2); a subsistence strategy is the culturally patterned way a group obtains food and other basic resources; each mode incorporates distinctive strategies for producing, exchanging, and consuming what people need to survive, and modes also organize society to get the necessary work done

foraging (gathering and hunting): one line — people rely on natural resources readily available in their environment, gathering fruits, nuts, berries, and roots, collecting honey, hunting and trapping wild animals, and fishing — with an original example (the Egan family of Ferngill)

honest note: foragers were once universal — gathering and hunting was practiced throughout the millions of years of hominin evolution, and plant cultivation and animal domestication took hold only around 10,000-12,000 years ago, so for the vast majority of human history every human being obtained food by gathering and hunting
horticulture: one line — small-scale plant cultivation with simple hand tools, intercropping, and rotating fallow plots — with an original example (the villagers of Ashcombe)

pastoralism: one line — the mode of subsistence associated with the care and use of domesticated herd animals, moving with herds in seasonal cycles — with an original example (the Salik family of the high steppe)
agriculture: one line — intensive plant cultivation with plows, draft animals, irrigation, and continuous cultivation of the same plots — with an original example (the farmers of Dunmere)

honest note: agriculture reshaped societies — greater yields and surplus support people who do not farm (specialists in craft, trade, religion, government), and villages grew into towns, cities, and regional empires; OpenStax also notes farming came with drawbacks

industrial food: one factual line — industrialism is the use of wage labor, machines, and chemical processes to mass-produce commodities; applied to food it means global production, with food processed and transported far from where it is eaten

honest framing: food is culture made edible — distinguishing what is and what is not food is a major cultural concern, food plays a major role in personal and cultural identity, and preparing and eating food properly requires cultural knowledge, artifacts, and rituals (OpenStax ch. 14)
supporting: most societies have a predominant mode of subsistence that incorporates practices from other modes
horticulture and agriculture are distinct strategies of plant cultivation; anthropologists reserve 'agriculture' for intensive methods
animal domestication emerged around the same time as plant cultivation; pastoralists treat herds as family property and often trade animal products for plant foods
foraging groups still exist today, often combining gathering and hunting with other strategies
outOfScope: distribution and exchange — reciprocity, redistribution, market exchange, gifts (sibling topic anthropology:foundations:economic-systems)
nutrition science — nutrients, diet and health effects of food (owned by the biology/nutrition subject)
market theory, food economics, and price formation (economics subject)
detailed ethnographies of specific subsistence peoples and colonial history of subsistence strategies (textbook depth, beyond one lesson)

claims.claim: Anthropologists define a mode of subsistence as the way that people interact with their environments in order to make a living; each mode incorporates distinctive strategies for producing, exchanging, and consuming the things people need to survive, and modes of subsistence also organize society to get the necessary work done.

Foraging (gathering and hunting) is a subsistence strategy in which people rely on the natural resources readily available in their environment — gathering fruits, nuts, berries, and roots, collecting honey from wild bees, hunting and trapping wild animals, and fishing in rivers and lakes.

Foragers were once universal: gathering and hunting was the strategy practiced throughout the millions of years of hominin evolution, while plant cultivation and animal domestication took hold only around 10,000-12,000 years ago, so for the vast majority of human history every human being obtained food by gathering and hunting; some peoples still practice this way of life today.

Horticulture is extensive, small-scale plant cultivation with simple hand tools: farmers clear plots, plant many crops side by side (intercropping), work the top layer of soil with digging sticks and hoes, and let plots lie fallow in rotation rather than cultivating the same land continuously.

Pastoralism is the mode of subsistence associated with the care and use of domesticated herd animals; pastoralists move with their herds in seasonal cycles, treat herds as family property passed down through generations, and often trade animal products for plant foods grown by neighboring farmers; animal domestication emerged around 10,000-12,000 years ago, about the same time as farming.

Agriculture (intensive agriculture) uses plows, draft animals, irrigation systems, and continuous cultivation of the same plots; it generates much greater yields than horticulture and supports far larger populations.

Honest note: agriculture reshaped societies — greater yields mean greater surplus, surplus supports people who do not have to farm, such as specialists in craft production, trade, religion, and government, and villages grew into towns and cities and, eventually, regional empires; OpenStax also notes that farming came with its share of drawbacks.

Industrialism is the use of wage labor, machines, and chemical processes to mass-produce commodities; it began developing in Britain in the 1700s, drew from and transformed other modes of subsistence, and spread to sweep the globe, so most food in industrial economies is mass-produced, processed, and transported far from where it is eaten.

Honest framing: food is culture made edible — distinguishing what is and what is not food is a major concern within and across most human cultures, food plays a major role in personal and cultural identity, food varies across societies, genders, classes, family groups, and seasons, and culturally appropriate preparation and consumption of food requires a vast array of knowledge, artifacts, and rituals.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How universal was foraging, and when did the other strategies begin?
positions: OpenStax 7.3 describes gathering and hunting as the strategy practiced throughout the millions of years of hominin evolution, with some peoples still practicing it today.
OpenStax 7.5 dates plant domestication to around 10,000-12,000 years ago, and OpenStax 7.4 dates animal domestication to the same period.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the honest note conservatively: foragers were once universal — for the vast majority of human history every human being obtained food by gathering and hunting — without citing a specific percentage, since the sources give time spans rather than a single figure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do 'subsistence' and 'economy' overlap, and where is the line between this topic and economic systems?
positions: OpenStax defines the economy as a system for making, circulating, and using things, and defines modes of subsistence as strategies for producing, exchanging, and consuming — the terms overlap.

The curriculum assigns distribution and exchange (reciprocity, redistribution, market exchange) to the sibling topic anthropology:foundations:economic-systems, and detailed subsistence study to this topic.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson covers how people obtain food and basic resources (the production side), with each strategy given one line plus an original example and the honest notes; distribution and exchange are deferred to the sibling economic-systems topic, and industrial food is covered here as a mode of subsistence, not as market theory.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the lesson making health or nutrition claims about foods?
positions: The biology-owned nutrition subject owns nutrition science: nutrients, dietary guidance, and health effects of food.
This lesson describes subsistence strategies factually and mentions foods (milk, cheese, rice, greens) only as examples of what strategies produce.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No nutritional or health claims appear in this lesson; foods are mentioned as cultural and subsistence facts only. Nutrition science is listed as out of scope.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no factual claims about subsistence: its in-30-seconds text ('Subsistence is a foundational concept in Anthropology...'), learning objectives, college version, vocabulary, Eli-10, worked example, common mistakes, and key takeaway were generic boilerplate (including the gate-banned 'label on a toolbox drawer' analogy and 'a college-level explanation names the concept' phrasing) with zero sources. All of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire machine-generated boilerplate draft with an evidence-based lesson.
Added the working definition of mode of subsistence, attributed to OpenStax 7.2, and the lesson's own subsistence-strategy definition.
Added the honest notes: foragers were once universal (supported by 7.3 + 7.5) and agriculture reshaped societies (supported by 7.5).

Added original (fictional) examples for every strategy: the Egan family of Ferngill (foraging), the villagers of Ashcombe (horticulture), the Salik family of the high steppe (pastoralism), the farmers of Dunmere (agriculture), and the dinner in Kestle (worked example).
Added the honest framing — food is culture made edible — supported by OpenStax's anthropology-of-food chapter (14-introduction).

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Existing registry id, reused with the identical URL. Read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL. Supports: the economy as the central way societies meet basic material needs and wants; anthropologists of all four fields study how people make a living — the framing in which subsistence study sits. Used as corroboration for the working-definition section.

sourceRecords.title: 7.2 Modes of Subsistence — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Existing registry id, reused with the identical URL. Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241204033258/...). Primary source of the working definition: 'Anthropologists have a term for the way that people interact with their environments in order to make a living: mode of subsistence'; the four main modes (gathering-hunting, pastoralism, plant cultivation, industrialism/post-industrialism); each mode incorporates distinctive strategies for producing, exchanging, and consuming; modes also organize society to get the necessary work done and emphasize certain ideals and values; most societies have a predominant mode that borrows from others.

sourceRecords.title: 7.3 Gathering and Hunting — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted (not in phase-2/phase-4 registries). Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241214140629/...). Supports: the gathering-hunting definition (relying on natural resources readily available in the environment; gathering fruits, nuts, berries, roots; collecting honey; hunting, trapping, fishing); 'Throughout the millions of years of hominin evolution, those living in such environments practiced a strategy known as gathering-hunting'; some peoples still practice this way of life; mobility, egalitarianism, and sharing as its social features; the word-order note that gathering provides the vast majority of calories.

sourceRecords.title: 7.4 Pastoralism — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted (not in phase-2/phase-4 registries). Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241208155839/...). Supports: pastoralism as 'the mode of subsistence associated with the care and use of domesticated herd animals'; living from milk, meat, hides, and other animal products; moving with herds in seasonal cycles over broad territory; herds as family property passed down to subsequent generations; pastoralists trading meat, milk, and animal products for the grains and vegetables grown by neighboring farmers; animal domestication developing around 10,000-12,000 years ago, about the same time as farming.

sourceRecords.title: 7.5 Plant Cultivation: Horticulture and Agriculture — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Existing registry id, reused with the identical URL. Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241202015414/...). Supports: plant domestication taking hold around 10,000-12,000 years ago; extensive horticulture (clearing plots, digging sticks and hoes, intercropping, fallow cycles, shifting cultivation) vs. intensive agriculture (plows, irrigation, continuous cultivation of the same plots); 'Intensive agriculture generates much greater yields than horticulture, supporting far larger populations'; greater yields mean greater surplus, supporting specialists in craft production, trade, religion, and government; villages growing into towns and cities and, eventually, regional empires; the honest line that 'farming came with its share of drawbacks as well'; anthropologists reserving 'agriculture' for intensive methods.

sourceRecords.title: 7.7 Industrialism and Postmodernity — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted (not in phase-2/phase-4 registries). Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241204033258/...). Supports: industrialism as 'the use of wage labor, machines, and chemical processes to mass-produce commodities'; beginning in the 1700s in Britain and growing to sweep the globe; industrialism drawing from and transforming other modes of subsistence (agriculture as a source of raw materials); the global economic system. Used for the one factual line on industrial food: mass production, processing, and global transport of food.

sourceRecords.title: 14 Introduction — Anthropology of Food (OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted (not in phase-2/phase-4 registries). Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20240601000000/...). Supports the honest framing: the study of food has a long history in anthropology; distinguishing what is and what is not food is a major concern within and across most human cultures; food varies across societies, genders, classes, family groups, and seasons; food plays a major role in personal and cultural identity; culturally appropriate preparation and consumption of food requires a vast array of knowledge, artifacts, and rituals. The lesson's phrase 'food is culture made edible' is the lesson's own framing of this material, not a quote.
